newsitem.title: USA: More strong growth, low inflation in US June NAPM.
newsitem.headline: More strong growth, low inflation in US June NAPM.

text.p: The June National Association of Purchasing Management report had more evidence of strong economic growth without any worrisome signs of inflation, economists said Tuesday.
After several strong regional reports were released Monday, expectations for an overwhelmingly robust national report mounted.
But the comprehensive gauge of activity in the manufacturing sector showed slight declines in most of its components, including the closely watched prices paid index.
"It's the same old story," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "There is ample evidence of strength in manufacturing and absolutely no sign of inflation."

The headline purchasing managers' index declined modestly to 55.7 percent in June from May's 57.1 reading, suggesting the manufacturing economy grew at a slightly slower pace during the month. Wall Street economists had expected a stronger reading of 56.4 percent.
A reading above 50 percent indicates growth in a sector, while a reading below 50 percent suggests contraction.
The prices paid index declined to 48.1 percent from 48.4 percent in June, and the inventories component fell to 43.2 percent from 47.6 percent.
All other components remained well above the 50 threshold, but failed to show the surging growth necessary to worry vigilant Fed policymakers, economists said.

"The NAPM index in the second quarter averaged much higher than it did in the first quarter, so on the growth side it shows that factory activity is very strong and is likely to remain strong," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
"I don't think the Fed will make a move until they see visible signs of inflation," he added.
The Federal Open Market Committee began a two-day meeting Tuesday and is widely expected to keep interest rates steady.
Wall Street pundits are sharply divided on whether the FOMC will hike interest rates 25 basis points or keep them unchanged at the next meeting in August.
Norbert Ore, chairman of the NAPM's business committee, said today a rise in interest rates could not be justified based on the report's inflation implications.
"We're not seeing any signs of inflation. And if the motivation for changes in interest rates is inflation, there aren't any signs in this report that we see," Ore said.

Ore said the survey suggested that manufacturers were optimistic about the performance of the economy in the second half of the year. But he added the manufacturing jobs market did not look strong over the long run.

"In the end, I think what it tells us is that manufacturing continues to do pretty well," said Stephen Slifer, chief U.S. economist at Lehman Brothers. "But the Fed needs to see hints that leading indicators of inflation are heating up...and there is nothing here that would lead you to think inflation will rise down the road."
